metadata.title: Do countries with high mean performance in PISA maintain their lead as students age?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD PISA in Focus brief uses published country-level mean performance from PISA (2000–2009 databases; Table A5.6) and links it to corresponding age-cohort mean literacy/numeracy performance from PIAAC (2011–2012). The analysis is presented at the level of country averages and age bands (e.g., 23–25, 26–28), rather than as an individual-student micro-data model. Because the document does not specify the use of complex survey weights or replicate-weight procedures, no weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) can be extracted. For analysts working with the underlying micro-data, OECD/IEA-style complex survey weights would typically be required to produce population-representative estimates, but this brief itself does not report a weighting implementation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent quantities in this brief are country-level mean scores (PISA and PIAAC) and their associations (e.g., R² in scatterplots), not student-level cognitive achievement outcomes derived from PISA plausible values. As a result, plausible-value generation/combination rules are not applicable to the reported analysis. Missing-data handling is not described because the brief relies on OECD-published summary statistics rather than reporting an original micro-data estimation procedure with an explicit missingness strategy.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The brief compares country-level mean performance of 15-year-olds in PISA waves (notably PISA 2000 and PISA 2003 for the shown scatterplots) with the corresponding PIAAC age-cohort mean literacy/numeracy scores for young adults aged 23–25 and 26–28 (three-year age bands used in PIAAC to increase reliability). It focuses on countries that participated in both PISA 2000 and PIAAC 2011–2012 (16 countries mentioned), and uses OECD-published PISA 2000–2009 database table outputs (Table A5.6) to align cohorts.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus brief links PISA performance at age 15 to adult literacy and numeracy performance measured in PIAAC for the same birth cohorts, using published country-level means rather than student-level predictive modeling. It reports positive associations between PISA reading/mathematics scores and PIAAC literacy/numeracy scores for corresponding age bands 12 years later, with scatterplot fit statistics such as R²≈0.3549 (PISA 2003 reading vs PIAAC 2012 literacy, ages 23–25) and R²≈0.4713 (PISA 2000 mathematics vs PIAAC 2012 numeracy, ages 26–28). The brief emphasizes that no country shows higher-than-expected adult performance relative to its PISA starting point, suggesting limited “catch-up” after compulsory schooling. It also notes that the relationship is not deterministic at the individual level and that cohort growth can vary substantially within countries (illustrated with Canada and Denmark retesting examples). Limitations include reliance on country averages, differences in country composition contributing to OECD averages across studies, and the fact that the analysis is descriptive/associational rather than causal.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is an OECD descriptive policy brief (PISA in Focus) that reports associations between published country-level mean scores from PISA and PIAAC. It does not present an original student-level ML pipeline, plausible-value estimation procedure, or an explicit missing-data handling method, so fields such as total_students, per-country analytic Ns, and ML techniques are not available from the provided text. The extraction therefore treats the work as exploratory/associational rather than an empirical predictive study.
